findings.message: HarbisonWalker, for industrial furnaces: "A stretcher course should never be used immediately below the skewback." Brick in these side walls is laid as stretchers, as in Olsen's insulating-brick kilns, whose featheredge skewbacks sit on a stretcher hot face (p.176, p.140). Where you can, lay the course under each skewback as headers.
findings.reference: kiln-hardware.md §4.1 [S20]; Olsen, The Kiln Book, 4th ed., p.176

findings.message: Brick counts assume dry joints at the nominal 9 × 4½ × 2½ in size, a ⅛ in saw cut, and 5 % extra for breakage. Each cut piece already takes its own brick in the count. The size is sourced; the saw cut is an assumption no source gives, so adjust it to your saw. The allowance is the masonry estimators' "at least 5 percent" (BIA): set allowances.brick in the design from your own experience. At the corners the side walls run through and the back and door fit between them, layer by layer.
findings.reference: 9 × 4½ × 2½ in straight; electric-and-thermal.md §5 [S54]; kerf assumed; brick-waste.md §1, BIA Technical Note 10 (2009), p.11 [W1]

findings.message: Fireboxes are built of the kiln's own layers, the walls' round their sides and over their roofs, the floor's under them; no source here gives a firebox its own lining. Against a wall, the grate sits its step below the chamber floor, so smouldering coals fall into the front stacking (p.188), and the inlet flues are cut at the floor's level in the wall between; below the kiln's floor the firebox has walls of its own. Stoke holes are cut with their foot at the grate (p.188), and ash pits are left open at the mouth (p.188). The roofs are drawn of the walls' layers laid flat: span a flat one with an arch, bricks or kiln shelves as Olsen does (p.145), or give it a corbel roof. Firebox 1, against the left wall, its 1 inlet flues don't fit side by side across it, so one opening its whole width is cut, roofed with a corbel, its courses stepped in over the top of its height, drawn with its grate level with the chamber floor, as no step is given.
findings.reference: Olsen, The Kiln Book, 4th ed., p.92, p.141, p.145, p.188

findings.message: Firebox 1: 18 in above the grate and an ash pit 9 in below it (33% of its height below the grate), the grate 0 in below the chamber floor. How high to set the grate depends on the firing wanted. Olsen sets it at the vertical midpoint (Fig. 8-2, p.199–200; the Breda kiln's equal volumes above and below, p.167); for the most heat his fast-fire kilns put more than half below, for the most air under the coals (p.140, p.204); a grate set too low chokes the coals (p.199). A 9–12 in rise from the grate to the chamber floor drops smouldering coals into the front stacking (p.188), and Fig. 7-3 steps up 12–15 in (p.179). Kilns fired for ash glazing and flashing make the firebox part of the first chamber, so the ash rides up round the pots: a step of 0 in, the default. This kiln is 16 ft³; Olsen's 12–18 in below and above is for 30–100 ft³ kilns (p.199), and the shortest he gives is 12½ in with the grate at 6–7 in, on a 12–16 ft³ fast-fire kiln.
findings.reference: Olsen, The Kiln Book, 4th ed., p.199–200 and Fig. 8-2 (the grate at the vertical midpoint; 12–18 in below and above on 30–100 ft³ kilns), p.188 (a 9–12 in rise from the grate to the chamber floor), p.179 (a 12–15 in step up)

findings.reference: Olsen, The Kiln Book, 4th ed., p.92, p.141, p.145, p.188

findings.message: Firebox 1: 18 in above the grate and an ash pit 9 in below it (33% of its height below the grate), the grate 0 in below the chamber floor. How high to set the grate depends on the firing wanted. Olsen sets it at the vertical midpoint (Fig. 8-2, p.199–200; the Breda kiln's equal volumes above and below, p.167); for the most heat his fast-fire kilns put more than half below, for the most air under the coals (p.140, p.204); a grate set too low chokes the coals (p.199). A 9–12 in rise from the grate to the chamber floor drops smouldering coals into the front stacking (p.188), and Fig. 7-3 steps up 12–15 in (p.179). Kilns fired for ash glazing and flashing make the firebox part of the first chamber, so the ash rides up round the pots: a step of 0 in, the default. This kiln is 16 ft³; Olsen's 12–18 in below and above is for 30–100 ft³ kilns (p.199), and the shortest he gives is 12½ in with the grate at 6–7 in, on a 12–16 ft³ fast-fire kiln.
findings.reference: Olsen, The Kiln Book, 4th ed., p.199–200 and Fig. 8-2 (the grate at the vertical midpoint; 12–18 in below and above on 30–100 ft³ kilns), p.188 (a 9–12 in rise from the grate to the chamber floor), p.179 (a 12–15 in step up)
